Sample details: N = 100 (50 obesity, 51 normal weight) (46.5% male), Baseline: 8–12 y.
Psychological variables: instruments: Depressive symptoms: CDI (Kovacs, 1992). Anxiety symptoms: STAIC (Spielberger et al ., 1973). Eating problems: ChEAT (Garner y Garfinkle, 1979).
Cofounder variables: Baseline BMI, Baseline psychological symptoms, Gender, Parental psychopathology, SES
Main findings: Higher BMI z-score at baseline was associated with greater eating symptomatology at follow-up ( β = 0.28, p < 0.05).

Psychological variables: instruments: Depressive symptoms: Short Mood and Feelings Questionnaire (Angold et al ., 1995).
Cofounder variables: Baseline BMI, Baseline depressive symptoms, Body dissatisfaction, Gender, SES
Main findings: Higher BMI at age 7 was associated with greater body dissatisfaction at age 11 ( β = 0.21, SE = 0.05, p < 0.001).

Weight status variable/measurement: BMI trajectory membership: nonoverweight p < 40, nonoverweigh p < 70, overweight/obesity, severe obesity. (M)
Psychological variables: instruments: Eating problems: EAT-26 general score and dieting subscale (Garner et al ., 1982)
Cofounder variables: Age, Ethnicity, Gender, Inhibitory control at 5 y, Pubertal status, Self-regulation at 5 y
Main findings: Youth on the severe obesity trajectory presented higher levels of general eating symptomatology at 15 years, followed by youth on the overweight/obese trajectories ( p < 0.5). Overweight/obesity (OR: 6.9, CI = 5.5–8.2), severe obesity (OR: 7.9, CI = 6.1–9.7). The restraint scale followed the same pattern: overweight/obesity (OR: 2.4, CI = 1.9–3.0), severe obesity (OR: 3.5, CI = 2.6–4.4). Female gender and higher pubertal status were associated with eating dysregulation ( p < 0.01).

Psychological variables: instruments: Depressive symptoms: Short Mood and Feelings Questionnaire (Angold et al ., 1995).
Cofounder variables: Age, Ethnicity, Gender, Parents’ educational level, School attended
Main findings: Boys: stable overweight or obesity was associated with later depressive symptomatology (b = 1.63, CI = 0.33–2.92).

Psychological variables: instruments: Major depressive disorder: DSM-III-R, through Diagnostic Interview Schedule for Children and Adolescents (Spitzer et al ., 1987)
Main findings: Obesity onset by 14 years old did not significantly predict the onset of MDD during late adolescence. Obesity that developed in late adolescence (14–20 years old) predicted MDD onset in early adulthood among females (OR = 5.89, CI = 2.31–15.01).
